one_liner: Header-only C++ JSON/CBOR/MessagePack/BSON library whose DOM reads ~2x and writes ~2-4x faster than nlohmann/json in the author's benchmark.
what_it_does: A header-only library for JSON and JSON-like formats (CBOR, MessagePack, BSON, UBJSON, CSV, TOON) with three ways to use the data: a mutable variant DOM (jsoncons::json keeps object keys sorted, ojson keeps insertion order), decode_json/encode_json into your own types via JSONCONS_*_TRAITS macros, and a StAX-style pull cursor with filters for texts too large to load. Extensions add JSON Pointer, Patch, Merge Patch, JSONPath, JMESPath and JSON Schema (drafts 4 to 2020-12). It is not a drop-in for nlohmann: the DOM model is similar (json::parse, operator[], dump), but accessors, iteration and the reflection macros have different names.
how_it_is_fast: The parser is a scalar, resumable, byte-at-a-time state machine that feeds a SAX-style visitor and reads streams in 16 KB chunks (no SIMD). The DOM decoder pushes members onto one flat stack and builds each object at end_object with a single std::sort on (key, index) into a sorted std::vector of key/value pairs, rather than allocating a std::map node per member; lookups are then std::lower_bound binary search. Values are 16 bytes: strings up to 13 chars are stored inline and longer strings take one header-plus-data allocation, which is why its DOM was among the smallest in the shootout (343 MB vs nlohmann 409 MB on the integer file). Doubles are printed with Grisu3, falling back to snprintf %.15g and then %.17g if the result does not round-trip, and parsed with std::from_chars where the config enables it.
when_to_use: You use nlohmann/json and want a mutable DOM that reads 1.8-2.1x and writes 1.8-3.9x faster (author's large-file test) without switching to an immutable-document library.
Mixed-format pipelines: the same basic_json value and reflection traits read and write JSON, CBOR (including typed arrays and stringref), MessagePack, BSON, UBJSON and CSV.
Multi-GB JSON or unbounded streams: json_stream_cursor pull-parses in 16 KB chunks, and pipe filters let you skip events, so you never build the whole tree.

You need JSONPath, JMESPath or JSON Schema validation in the same dependency. Compiled expressions and json_schema objects are documented as immutable and thread-safe, so they can be shared across threads.
Memory-bound DOM work: the parsed 540 MB integer file took 343 MB, against nlohmann 409, Boost.JSON 502 and yyjson 871 MB in the same run. RapidJSON used a little less (332 MB).
when_not_to_use: Raw parse/serialize throughput is the goal. In the author's own shootout, yyjson reads the integer file 3.9x faster (1.007 s vs 3.918 s), and RapidJSON, Boost.JSON and glaze also read faster.

Building big objects by random-order insertion: json stores objects as a sorted vector, so each insert shifts elements. A user benchmark in issue #346 (still open) measured 1000 insert+erase at 11.75 ms vs nlohmann's 0.47 ms. ojson avoids sorting, but its find() is a linear scan.

Float-heavy input built with toolchains outside the std::from_chars auto-detection (GCC 11+ or MSVC 19.24+, C++17), where double parsing falls back to strtod. Separately, the 2016 nativejson-benchmark (clang 7) had an old jsoncons parsing canada.json slower than nlohmann (77.3 vs 55.6 ms).

You need a stable API. Recent minor releases renamed public types (1.9.0: string_source, order_preserving_policy, json_conv_traits; 1.8.0: json_pointer_arg), and 1.8.0 changed the basic_json copy constructor from shallow to deep copies of json_ref pointers, so pin a version.

integration.dependencies: none (vcpkg port available; the optional extensions are in include/jsoncons_ext)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11. The std::from_chars number path needs C++17 with GCC 11+ or MSVC 19.24+, and the pmr:: aliases need std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator. README CI matrix: VS2019/2022, GCC 6-12, clang 3.9-15, Xcode 11-14.
integration.platforms: any. Portable scalar code; the only intrinsics are optional F16C (half floats) and MSVC BMI2 mulx. CI runs on Windows x86/x64, Ubuntu x64 and macOS.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for basic_json, parsers or encoders. Compiled JSONPath/JMESPath expressions and json_schema are documented as immutable and thread-safe.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same model (mutable variant DOM; json sorts keys like nlohmann::json's std::map, ojson keeps insertion order), but accessor, iteration and reflection APIs differ, so call sites need porting

gotchas: Duplicate keys: the parsed json keeps the first occurrence. {"first":1,"second":2,"first":3} yields first == 1 (test parse_duplicate_names).
Lenient by default: allow_comments defaults to true, so /* */ and // comments are silently accepted. Set allow_comments(false) in json_options for strict parsing. max_nesting_depth defaults to 1024.
lossless_bignum defaults to true, so integers beyond 64 bits come back as strings tagged semantic_tag::bigint, and out-of-range floats as bigdec, not as doubles.
Errors are reported by exceptions (only some APIs return std::error_code). With -fno-exceptions or JSONCONS_NO_EXCEPTIONS, every throw becomes std::terminate.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick jsoncons over yyjson, simdjson or Boost.JSON when you want one header-only dependency that covers a mutable DOM, struct mapping, pull streaming, the binary formats (CBOR/MessagePack/BSON) and JSONPath/JMESPath/Schema, with a DOM under half the size of yyjson's in the author's test. If you only need fast JSON parse/serialize, yyjson (3.9x faster read here), simdjson (read-only parsing) or Boost.JSON (1.7x faster read here) are the better picks.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's own json_benchmarks (single run; MSVC 17.14.16 /O2 /Ot /std:c++23preview; Lenovo ThinkPad X Extreme, CPU model not stated), parsing a 540.82 MB text+integer file from std::ifstream into jsoncons::json took 3.918 s vs 8.177 s for nlohmann::json (2.1x), and writing took 0.744 s vs 2.885 s (3.9x). On the 794.72 MB text+double file it was 8.879 s / 3.879 s vs 15.997 s / 7.165 s (1.8x both ways), and the same pages show yyjson, RapidJSON and Boost.JSON beating jsoncons on both read and write.
status_note: Actively maintained (v1.9.0 released 2026-08-07, commits through 2026-09-22, OSS-Fuzz integrated, no NVD CVEs found for 'jsoncons'), and header-only under the Boost Software License 1.0, so you can vendor it by copying include/jsoncons (plus include/jsoncons_ext for the extensions).
